## Why

Scanning a store's directory board was meant to teach the app the store's layout in
one shot. Measured against the five live stores, it does the opposite.

| Store | Aisles | From scan | Standard | Manual |
|-------|--------|-----------|----------|--------|
| Walmart | 18 | 0 | 18 | 0 |
| WorstFoods | 18 | 0 | 18 | 0 |
| Whole Foods | 20 | 0 | 18 | 2 |
| ShopRite | **38** | **20** | 18 | 0 |
| Stop&Shop | **39** | **21** | 18 | 0 |

The three stores never scanned have a clean set of eighteen departments. The two
that were scanned carry roughly double that, because **a scan does not replace the
departments — it adds a second, overlapping set on top of them.**

ShopRite ends up with aisle 16 (*Milk, Natural Dairy, Orange Juice*) *and* a Dairy
& Eggs department. Stop&Shop has aisles 20 and 21 holding frozen goods *and* a
Frozen department. Milk has two legitimate homes, so it lands in whichever one the
matcher saw last. The duplicate-section bug fixed earlier this month was this,
treated at the display layer.

About one in seven extracted aisles is unusable and permanent:

- Stop&Shop — `Three` → picante sauce (the printed word "three" read as an aisle
  id), `Florist-19` → logs
- ShopRite — `6,9` → Scalafani, `6,11` → Salsa, `9,16` → Stuffing,
  `Beer Garden` → Water 5 Gallon

A harness run against the shipping prompt (`scratchpad/ocr_check.py`) also showed
the model inventing an aisle number that was not on the sign, deterministically at
temperature 0, by copying the prompt's own worked example.

The deeper problem is that **the plaque is not a reliable input.** One ShopRite has
printed boards; another has a touchscreen kiosk. Whole Foods labels departments by
name with no numbers at all. A photograph cannot capture what the store did not
print, and the layout changes whenever a manager rearranges a bay.

## What replaces it

Capture one aisle at a time, from ground truth, at the moment it is worth
capturing.

> You are in ShopRite. The next item on your list is deodorant, and it is in the
> unsorted bucket. You look it up however that store lets you — board, kiosk, or
> asking someone. You tap the item, say "aisle sixteen", confirm, and move on.

The aisle is created **as a side effect of the assignment.** There is no step where
you first declare that aisle 16 exists. That inversion is the whole feature.

This works at every store, because the input is the shopper, not the signage.

### Explicitly not in scope

**In-aisle position.** An earlier draft captured "international, *middle*". Cut:
the position is not printed on any plaque, it changes when a manager rearranges the
bay, and a shopper standing in the aisle simply looks. Storing it would age badly
and buy nothing.

**Anything AI beyond transcription.** Turning "aisle sixteen" into `16` is string
handling, not inference. See [Parsing](#parsing).

## The flow

1. In At Store mode, every item in the unsorted bucket gets an inline
   **Where is this?** control. It cannot be the row tap: in At Store mode a tap
   crosses the item off, swipes move it to suggestions and back, and long-press is
   the delete menu (`GroceryItemRow.swift:86-148`). The whole gesture budget is
   spent, so capture needs its own visible control.
   Already-mapped rows do **not** carry the chip — correcting a wrong aisle is rare
   and goes in the long-press menu beside Delete. Long-press is wrong for the
   unsorted bucket precisely because it is undiscoverable, which is the complaint
   Map Aisles drew.
2. Tapping it opens a small sheet: a microphone button and a text field. Both
   produce the same string; the keyboard is the fallback when it is loud.
3. Speech is recognised **on-device** by `SFSpeechRecognizer` with
   `requiresOnDeviceRecognition = true` — see [Why not Whisper](#why-not-whisper).
4. The transcript is normalised into an aisle label and **shown back before it is
   written.** Never committed on the strength of the transcription alone.
5. On confirm: resolve or create the aisle, write the mapping, dismiss. The item
   moves out of the unsorted bucket into its section.

The confirm step is not optional. Any recogniser confuses "sixteen" and "sixty" in a
noisy shop, and this app has already shipped a fix for a transcriber emitting "Thank
you for watching" over near-silence. Showing the parse and taking a tap is the same
rule already applied to dictated lists.

### Why not Whisper {#why-not-whisper}

The app's existing `SpeechDictationService` posts audio to the `transcribeAudio`
mutation, which calls OpenAI Whisper in a Lambda. That is the wrong tool here.

- **The premise of this feature is bad signal.** You are deep inside a shop. Whisper
  needs record → upload → Lambda → OpenAI → back. On-device recognition needs no
  network and returns as you speak.
- **`contextualStrings` biases recognition toward words you supply.** Feed it
  "aisle", the number words, and the store's existing aisle names, and the
  sixteen/sixty problem largely goes away. Whisper offers no equivalent hook.
- **Free**, with no OpenAI key anywhere in the path.

Cost: `import Speech` (unused in the project today), a new
`NSSpeechRecognitionUsageDescription`, a one-time permission prompt on top of the
microphone one, and a `supportsOnDeviceRecognition` check with a fallback to typing
where it is unavailable. Deployment target is iOS 17.0, well within range.

**Whisper stays for bulk list dictation.** Long, messy, free-form speech — "two
pounds of chicken, some of that sourdough, oh and kitchen roll" — is the case
Whisper is good at, and it already works. Different job, different tool.

## Parsing {#parsing}

Deterministic, on-device, no model call. In order:

1. Trim, collapse whitespace, strip a trailing full stop.
2. **Truncate at the first comma.** "International, middle" → "International".
   Without this the store gains an aisle literally named *International, Middle* —
   the same junk class as the `Pasta · Pasta Sauce` heading the OCR prompt
   produced.
3. Strip a leading "aisle" / "in aisle" / "it's in".
4. Map number words to digits, zero through thirty ("sixteen" → `16`). The
   recogniser returns digits for some utterances and words for others; both must
   land in the same place or the store gets a `16` *and* a `Sixteen`.
5. If what remains is a bare integer → a **numbered aisle**, `number` = the digits.
6. Otherwise → a **named aisle**, Title Cased, `name` = the string.
7. Match against the store's existing aisles through `AisleNaming.match` before
   creating anything. Aisle 16 entered twice must not become two aisles, and
   "dairy" must resolve to the existing Dairy & Eggs department rather than
   creating a rival.

Rejected input: empty after normalisation, or longer than ~40 characters (a
sentence, not an aisle). Say so in the sheet and keep the text for editing rather
than discarding it.

## Data model

### The blocking gap

`ProductAisleMapping` already has the right field:

```
userAisleOverride: a.string()   // null = use LLM suggestion
```

`ProductAisleMapping.swift:33` resolves `userAisleOverride ?? aisleId`, so a user
value already wins at read time. **But the write path cannot set it.** The
`upsertProductAisleMapping` mutation (`resource.ts:563`) takes no such argument, and
the resolver (`upsertProductAisleMapping.js`) never writes it. Anything saved today
goes into `aisleId` — the field phases 4 and 5 of inference overwrite.

So a hand-captured aisle would survive until the next inference run and then
silently revert. This must be fixed first or the feature is a lie.

**Change:** add `userAisleOverride: a.string()` to the mutation arguments and a
corresponding conditional `SET` in the resolver, matching the existing pattern for
`confidence`, `source`, and `reasoning`. Then `StoreService.upsertMapping` gains the
parameter and the capture sheet passes it.

### Provenance

`MappingSource` is currently `['IMAGE', 'LLM_GUESS']`. Add `USER_SIGHTED` so
"why is this here?" has an honest answer and so inference can be told to leave these
alone. Enum values are additive; existing rows keep decoding.

### Aisle creation

`StoreService.addAisle(to:number:name:)` (`StoreService.swift:314`) already appends a
`StoreAisle` and saves the store. Reuse it unchanged. New aisles land at the end of
`displayOrder`; the existing drag-to-reorder screen is how they get into walk order.

## What was deleted {#deleted}

| Path | Lines |
|------|-------|
| `GroceryApp/Views/AisleScanSheet.swift` | 834 |
| `amplify/data/aisleExtractionJobHandler/` | 1,557 |
| `GroceryApp/Services/AisleExtractionService.swift` | — |
| `AisleExtractionJob` model + stream wiring | — |
| Aisle photo S3 bucket and its grants | — |

Done in `7d4950d` — 3,215 lines removed. Two consequences worth naming:

- **The S3 Lambda-broker problem disappears.** Photos are the only thing in that
  bucket; with nothing uploading, there is nothing to scope.
- **The largest AI cost in the app goes with it.** A scan is a multi-image vision
  call plus up to four batched follow-up phases.
- **The camera and photo-library permissions stay.** An earlier draft of this spec
  claimed they went with the scan. Wrong — item photos use both. Only their usage
  strings changed, from describing directory scanning to describing what they are
  actually for.

Retain `inferProductAisleFunction` — it works from the store's aisle list, not from
OCR, and it is what places items into departments without any capture at all.

## Migrating the two scanned stores {#migration}

*Done 2026-08-31. Recorded as run.*

41 OCR-derived aisles exist across ShopRite and Stop&Shop, with mappings pointing at
them. Leaving them makes the new feature look broken on the two stores actually in
use.

1. Snapshot both `HouseholdStore` rows and all `ProductAisleMapping` rows for them.
   PITR covers the tables, but a scoped snapshot is cheaper to reason about.
2. Drop aisles whose id begins with `aisle-` **and** whose label is junk — the six
   named above, plus any whose `number` is not a bare integer.
3. For surviving numbered aisles, keep them: aisle 12 at Stop&Shop is real and
   correct, and re-learning twenty aisles by voice is not a reasonable ask.
4. Blank the `name` on every retained OCR aisle. They currently hold shelf-tag
   dumps — *"mops, moth balls, oven cleaner…"* — and the section header is meant to
   say which aisle, not what is in it. The contents stay in `description`, which is
   what inference reads.
5. Repoint mappings whose aisle was dropped at the matching standard department,
   or clear them so the item returns to the unsorted bucket.

This was a deliberate, case-by-case job against named tables with the live household
on a protect list, per `CLAUDE.md`. What actually happened:

| | ShopRite | Stop&Shop |
|---|---|---|
| Aisles before | 38 | 39 |
| Junk dropped | 4 — `6,9`, `6,11`, `9,16`, `Beer Garden` | 2 — `Florist-19`, `Three` |
| Aisles after | 34 | 37 |

11 mappings pointed at the dropped aisles and were deleted, returning those items to
the unsorted bucket. Every retained scan aisle had its shelf-tag dump moved out of
`name` and into `description`, so section headers say which aisle rather than what is
on the shelf. Final check: 1,306 mappings, **0 orphaned**.

One trap worth recording. The first orphan check compared each mapping's aisle
against the set of aisle *ids* and reported 949 orphans. Mappings store the aisle
*number* just as often — `AisleNaming.match` resolves id, name **or** number — so the
check was wrong, not the data. Re-run with the app's own rule it found 11, exactly
the mappings belonging to the six dropped aisles.

## Tests

Unit, no network:

- Number words zero through thirty, each to its digit.
- "aisle sixteen", "Aisle 16", "16", "it's in aisle 16" all resolve to the same
  aisle.
- "International, middle" → `International`.
- "dairy" resolves to the existing `standard-dairy`, not a new aisle.
- Entering the same aisle twice creates one aisle.
- Empty and over-long input are rejected without writing.

Against the deployed stack:

- A capture survives a subsequent inference run — the regression the
  `userAisleOverride` gap would otherwise cause.
- A capture made with no signal queues and applies on reconnect, like every other
  mutation.

## Open questions

1. **Does a numbered store still want department headers?** ShopRite would show
   both "16" and "Personal Care" until every item is captured. Probably fine — the
   unsorted bucket shrinks as you go — but it is the first thing to look at in real
   use.
2. **Should inference stop guessing once a store has captured aisles?** Partly
   answered: inference now reads `userAisleOverride` in preference to `aisleId`
   and drops the stale confidence score that came with the guess, so what a person
   saw is what the model learns from. Whether a sighting should suppress guessing
   for neighbouring items is still open.
3. **Quick Trip is unaffected** — no store, no aisles. Confirm nothing in the
   capture path assumes a store exists.
